title: Project Proposal Specs
text:
Each player unit fires a coded IR packet when the trigger is pressed.
FPGA generates a 38 kHz IR carrier, verified with an oscilloscope capture.
A player unit registers a hit on its single hit zone when struck by the other player’s blaster from at least 5 m indoors.
IR receiver input is passed through a synchronizer before being decoded on the FPGA.
Hits are not registered from a player’s own shots or from stray IR sources (e.g., a TV remote).

title: Project Proposal Specs
text:
Game Logic and Data

Excellence

Game progresses through start, play, out, and game over states, with a reset returning both units to start.
A valid hit decrements the hit player’s health.
SPI interconnect between the MCU and FPGA is wired correctly and transfers hit events (shooter ID) and game state.
MCU handles hit events with an interrupt rather than polling.

title: Project Proposal Specs
text:
Display and Audio Feedback

Excellence

An indicator LED flashes on a valid hit.
MCU plays sampled sound effects through its DAC, with sample timing driven by a hardware timer.
A hit sound effect plays on each valid hit.
LED display animations are stored in SPRAM and played back on command from the MCU.
Distinct sound effects play for firing, hits, and win/lose.

title: Project Proposal Specs
text:
Web Server and Scoreboard

Excellence

MCU sends hit events to the ESP8266 over UART, and the ESP8266 delivers them to the laptop server.
Laptop server logs hit events from both player units.
Games can be started and reset from the scoreboard web page.

title: Project Proposal Specs
text:
Hardware and Power

Excellence

Both units run untethered on battery power inside 3D-printed housings with straps.
A full 5-minute two-player game runs on battery.

title: E155 Final Project
text: We will build a two-player infrared laser tag system in which each player carries a blaster and a wearable target, both driven by one E155 development board (iCE40 UP5K FPGA + STM32L432KC MCU). Pulling the trigger fires a coded IR packet; when another player’s receivers decode it, their unit registers a hit, flashes its LEDs, plays a sound effect, and reports the hit over Wi-Fi to a laptop scoreboard.

title: Project Proposal
text:
FPGA Design Details
The FPGA handles everything that needs precise timing:

IR transmitter: divides the 48 MHz internal oscillator down to a 38 kHz carrier. When the MCU sends a fire command over SPI, a packet encoder FSM gates the carrier into marks and spaces and drives the IR LED through a transistor.
IR receiver decoder: each receiver output passes through a two-flop synchronizer into a pulse-width FSM. The FSM detects the start burst, decodes the bits, and checks that the second half of the packet is the inverse of the first. A valid packet is latched together with the index of the receiver that caught it, and an interrupt line to the MCU is raised.
LED pattern engine: hit/win/lose animations are stored in single-port RAM (SPRAM) and played back at a fixed frame rate. The MCU picks the pattern over SPI. (SPRAM is not used in any lab.)

title: Project Proposal
text:
MCU Design Details
The MCU runs the game logic, audio, and communication:

Trigger: the push button is a GPIO input with an external interrupt (EXTI), debounced with a timer. A cooldown limits the fire rate.
SPI master to FPGA: sends fire and pattern commands. On the FPGA’s interrupt line, the MCU reads the hit packet and the receiver index and ignores its own player ID. Damage depends on which receiver was hit (for example, more for chest or back than for a shoulder) and is subtracted from health.
Audio: a basic timer (TIM6) triggers the on-chip digital-to-analog converter (DAC) through DMA at 16 kHz, playing 8-bit sound samples stored in flash. The output goes through an LM386 amplifier to the speaker. (The DAC is not used in any lab.)
Wi-Fi: UART at 115200 baud to the ESP8266. Hit events go out to the scoreboard. When one player’s health reaches zero, the scoreboard sends a game-over message back so the other unit plays its win sound.
